questions.question: A 42-year-old male presents with complaints of lower back pain radiating down his left leg, associated with numbness over the top of his foot and difficulty in dorsiflexing his big toe. On examination, he has weakness in the extension of the great toe and decreased sensation along the dorsum of the foot. Reflexes are normal. Based on the symptoms, which vertebral level is most likely affected?

explanation.text: The patient's symptoms suggest nerve root compression, commonly caused by a herniated disc. The key findings in this case include lower back pain radiating down the left leg, numbness over the top of the foot, and weakness in dorsiflexion of the great toe (extensor hallucis longus), without reflex abnormalities. These are classic signs of L5 nerve root involvement.

L5 nerve root compression, often due to L4-L5 disc herniation, results in: Weakness in great toe dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus). Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Radiating pain down the lateral aspect of leg. Slipped disc: A herniated disc, also known as a slipped disc, occurs when the soft center (nucleus pulposus) of a spinal disc pushes through a tear in the tougher exterior (annulus fibrosus) and presses on nearby nerves.

questions.question: A 2-year-old child is brought in for a routine check-up. The parents have noticed a pronounced lumbar curvature since the child began walking. Which of the following best describes this lumbar curvature?

options.D: Curvature related to increased abdominal weight

explanation.text: Lumbar lordosis is a secondary curvature that becomes evident in infancy as the child begins to assume upright posture, stand and walk, contributing to normal posture development. Vertebral Curvature: Vertebral column in adults has 4 curvatures: Cervical lordosis Thoracic kyphosis Lumbar lordosis Sacral kyphosis Types of Vertebral Curvature: Primary Curvature Secondary Curvature Developmental.

Thoracic and sacral kyphosis (both concave anteriorly) are primary curvatures. (Option A & C) Develop during the fetal period in response to the flexed fetal position. Are in the same direction as the main curvatures of the fetal vertebral column. Retained throughout life due to differences in height between the anterior and posterior parts of the vertebrae. Acquired in relation to the erect human posture.

Cervical and lumbar lordosis (both concave posteriorly) are secondary curvatures. Result from extension from the flexed fetal position. Begin to appear during the late fetal period but do not become obvious until infancy (roughly, 1st year). Secondary curvatures are primarily maintained by differences in the thickness between the anterior and posterior parts of the intervertebral (IV) discs.

Cervical lordosis becomes evident when an infant begins to raise (extend) the head while prone and to hold the head up while sitting. Lumbar lordosis appears when toddlers (children learning to walk) begin to assume upright posture, standing and walking.

It is more pronounced in females. (Option B) Functional Importance: Curvatures of the vertebral column enhance flexibility (shock-absorbing resilience), augmenting the passive flexibility provided by the intervertebral (IV) discs. Response to Increased Load: When bearing heavy loads (e.g., carrying a heavy backpack), both the IV discs and curvatures are compressed, increasing the curvature.

Impact of Additional Anterior Weight: Carrying weight in front of the body’s normal gravitational axis (e.g., large breasts, obesity, pregnancy, or carrying a child) tends to increase these curvatures. (Option D)

questions.question: A patient has restricted spinal rotation and lateral flexion. Which vertebral structure primarily functions as a lever for these movements?

explanation.text: Transverse processes project laterally from the pediculolaminar junctions and serve as levers for muscles and ligaments mainly involved in spinal rotation and lateral flexion. Typical Vertebra Has a ventral body, dorsal arch with processes, and a vertebral foramen. Image Vertebral Body Adjacent vertebral bodies are connected by fibrocartilage discs. Form a flexible, weight-supporting central axis.

Transmits even greater forces generated from attached muscles. Vertebral Arch Consists of pedicles and a broader laminae. Transverse, superior, and inferior articular processes project from the junction of the pedicle and lamina. Vertebral Foramina Formed by the vertebral arch and body. Contains the spinal cord, meninges and their vessels. Intervertebral Foramina Located between adjoining vertebrae, near junctions of vertebral bodies and arches.
Transmit mixed spinal nerves, small recurrent nerves, and blood and lymphatic vessels.

**Spinous Processes (Option A):** Project dorsally from the junction of the lamina. Act as levers for muscles that control posture and active movements (flexion/extension, lateral flexion and rotation) of the vertebral column.

**Transverse Processes (Option D):** Project laterally from the pediculolaminar junctions. Serve as levers for muscles and ligaments, mainly concerned with rotation and lateral flexion. Articular Processes (Option B & C) Superior articular processes project cranially with dorsal facets; inferior articular processes project caudally with ventral facets. They form zygapophysial or facet joints and form part of the posterior boundaries of intervertebral foramina, permitting only limited vertebral movement. Trabecular Structure Vertebrae are internally composed of trabecular bone with an outer shell of compact bone perforated by vascular foramina. Trabecular interior contains red bone marrow and basivertebral veins.

questions.question: An anatomy professor presents an image of a vertebra in class and asks the students to identify its type. Which type of vertebra is depicted in the image?

explanation.text: Lumbar vertebrae are characterized by their large size, thick and horizontal spinous processes, and the absence of transverse foramina (which are present in cervical vertebrae) or costal facets (which are found in thoracic vertebrae).

**Feature Cervical Vertebrae (Option A):** Thoracic Vertebrae (Option B) Lumbar Vertebrae (Option C) Image Size Small size Intermediate-size Large size Body Small, broad with a convex anterior surface. Waisted cylinder; nearly equal transverse and AP dimensions. Wider transversely Vertebral Canal Triangular Small and circular Triangular Pedicles and Laminae Pedicles: Attach midway between the discal surface of the vertebral body. Lamina: Thin, slightly curved. Pedicles: Do not diverge as the vertebral foramen is small and circular Lamina: Short, thick, and broad. Pedicles: Short Laminae: Broad and short. Spinous Process Short, bifid with two unequal tubercles. Slants downward. Almost horizontal, quadrangular, and thickened along its posterior and inferior borders. Transverse Process Composite structure Large, club-like. Long, thin. Superior Articular Facets Flat and ovoid, directed superoposteriorly. Directed posteriorly and slightly superolaterally. Bear vertical concave facets facing posteromedially. Inferior Articular Facets Directed mainly anteriorly. Directed forwards and slightly superomedially. Have vertical convex articular facets facing anterolaterally. Special Features Foramen Transversarium: Transmits the vertebral artery and vein, and a branch from the cervicothoracic ganglion (vertebral nerve) except in the seventh cervical vertebra. Have lateral costal facets and transverse process facets for rib articulation. Costal facets and transverse foramina are absent.
**Sacral vertebrae (Option D):** are not considered individually because they fuse into a single immobile sacrum during adolescence, typically formed from five segments.

questions.question: A 35-year-old patient undergoes spinal surgery. Postoperatively, he develops a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Which space is most likely compromised?

explanation.text: The subarachnoid space, which contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), is likely compromised after spinal surgery due to potential puncture of the dura or arachnoid.

**Epidural Space (Option A):** Subdural Space Subarachnoid Space Located between the spinal dura mater and the periosteum. Contains: Loose areolar tissue Semiliquid fat Spinal arteries supplying deeper structures Internal vertebral venous plexus. Epidural anesthesia is given here Potential space between the dura and arachnoid mater. (Option B) Contains a thin layer of serous fluid. Allows movement of the dura over the arachnoid. Extends onto spinal nerves and connects with lymphatic spaces. Wide space between pia mater and arachnoid mater. Filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). (Option C) Cushions the brain and spinal cord. Wider in the spinal region, especially below the spinal cord where it encloses the cauda equina. Lumbar punctures are typically performed between L3 & L4 vertebrae.
**Periosteal space (Option D):** is not a recognized anatomical space for CSF.

questions.question: A patient undergoes a procedure affecting a delicate, thread-like structure extending from the conus medullaris to the coccyx as marked in the figure. Which of the following statements regarding this structure is correct?

options.A: It is composed mainly of dura mater and contains no nerve fibers
options.B: Distal part of it is called the coccygeal ligament.
options.C: It does not extend beyond the sacral hiatus
options.D: It measures about 50 cm in length

explanation.text: The marked structure in the given image is the Filum terminale and it consists of 2 parts: filum terminale internum and the distal filum terminale externum, also known as the coccygeal ligament.

**Filum terminale is a thread-like extension of the pia mater (Option A):** measuring about 20 cm in length. (Option D) Location: Extends from the tip of the conus medullaris to the base of the coccyx. Pathway:

**Pierces the dural tube, traverses the sacral canal and sacral hiatus (Option C):** and attaches to the dorsal surface of the first coccygeal vertebra. Segments Filum Terminale Internum: Approximately 15 cm long, located within the dural sac. Filum Terminale Externum: About 5 cm long, situated outside the dura mater, below the second sacral vertebra. Composition: Primarily pia mater, with some nerve fibers from the second and third coccygeal nerves on its outer surface. The central canal of the spinal cord extends into it for about 5 mm.

questions.question: The movements at the _______ joint permit a person to look to the right and left

explanation.text: Atlanto-axial joint: The Atlanto-axial joint is formed between the atlas (C1 vertebra) and the axis (C2 vertebra) in the spine. This joint is responsible for rotational movements of the head. The axis (C2) has a peg-like structure called the dens or odontoid process, which fits into the atlas (C1), allowing for rotation. Therefore, the Atlanto-axial joint permits the specific movements required for looking to the right and left.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Atlanto-occipital joint The Atlanto-occipital joint permits flexion and extension movements of the head, like nodding. It's mainly for tilting the head forward and backward, rather than side-to-side rotation.

Option C - C2-C3 intervertebral joint The C2-C3 intervertebral joint permits flexion, extension, lateral bending, and some degree of rotation, but sideways rotation is mainly handled by the Atlanto-axial joint, not C2-C3. Option D - C3-C4 intervertebral joint The C3-C4 joint, similar to C2-C3, allows neck movements like flexion, extension, lateral bending, and some degree of rotation.
However, it's not directly involved in sideways rotational movements.

questions.question: Retraction of the scapula is primarily done by?

explanation.text: Trapezius: The trapezius muscle is a large muscle that covers the upper back and neck. It plays a key role in the movement and stabilization of the scapula. The middle and lower fibers of the trapezius muscle primarily perform scapular retraction, which involves pulling the scapula backward toward the spine.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Serratus anterior: The serratus anterior muscle protracts and rotates the scapula, stabilizing it against the ribcage. However, it doesn't directly retract the scapula at the sternoclavicular

joint. Option C - Subscapularis: The subscapularis muscle, part of the rotator cuff, sits on the front of the scapula. It internally rotates the humerus and stabilizes the shoulder joint but doesn't aid in scapular retraction. Option D - Supraspinatus: The supraspinatus muscle, part of the rotator cuff, is located on the back of the scapula. It helps initiate shoulder abduction but isn't mainly responsible for scapular retraction.

questions.question: What is the cause of scapular winging?

explanation.text: Serratus anterior: The serratus anterior muscle is primarily responsible for stabilizing the scapula against the thoracic wall. When the serratus anterior muscle is paralyzed or weakened, it can lead to winging of the scapula. This muscle is especially important for maintaining proper scapular position during movements such as pushing, pulling, and reaching. Hence, option B is correct.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Trapezius: The trapezius muscle stabilizes and moves the scapula, but its paralysis typically doesn't cause scapular winging. Option C - Latissimus dorsi: The latissimus dorsi muscle assists in various shoulder movements but is typically not associated with scapular winging, even when weakened or paralyzed.
Option D - Pectoralis major: The pectoralis major muscle aids shoulder movements but usually doesn't cause scapular winging if paralyzed.

questions.question: Ligamentum flavum has high levels of:-

explanation.text: The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent vertebrae, crucial for spinal stability and flexibility. Elastin fibers within it provide elasticity, enabling stretching and recoiling to maintain stability during movement. Its yellowish color comes from high elastin levels.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Type 1 collagen: Type 1 collagen is abundant in tendons, ligaments, and bone, but the ligamentum flavum contains lower levels compared to other connective tissues. Option B - Type 2 collagen: Type 2 collagen is primarily found in hyaline cartilage, like in joint articular cartilage and vertebral discs, but it's not notably present in the ligamentum flavum.
Option C - Reticular fibers: Reticular fibers, composed of type 3 collagen, form mesh-like networks in organs like lymph nodes and spleen, but they're not notably present in the ligamentum flavum.

questions.question: Which of the following is normally seen in lumbar spine?

explanation.text: Lordosis: Lordosis refers to the inward curvature of the spine, creating a concave shape. In the lumbar spine, lordosis is considered a normal anatomical feature. It helps to maintain the balance and proper alignment of the spine, allowing for efficient weight distribution and movement.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Scoliosis: Scoliosis is an abnormal sideways curvature of the spine, typically found in the thoracic or thoracolumbar regions, not the lumbar spine. Option B - Kyphosis: Kyphosis is an excessive forward curvature of the spine, often causing a rounded or hunched-back appearance. While normal in the thoracic spine, it's uncommon in the lumbar spine.
Option D - Recurvatum: Recurvatum is hyperextension of a joint, seen notably in the knee but not typically in the lumbar spine.
